title: Body & health
goal: Name parts of the body, say what hurts and how you feel, understand a doctor's advice, and say what someone should or shouldn't do.
intro:
In Marathi, aches and illnesses aren't things you 'have' so much as things that happen to you: **माझं डोकं दुखतंय** 'my head is hurting', **मला ताप आहे** 'to me there is fever', **मला सर्दी झाली** 'a cold has happened to me'.

You'll also learn the 'should' form of the verb (करावं, घ्यावं), which doctors, parents and grandmothers use a lot.

vocab.note: n · पोटात दुखतंय 'I have a stomach ache'
The body part is the subject: माझा पाय दुखतोय.
Dative: मला बरं वाटतंय 'I feel well'; मला वाटतं 'I think'.
f · उलटी होतेय 'I feel like vomiting / am vomiting'
m · respectful plural: डॉक्टरांना, डॉक्टर आले
f · काळजी घ्या 'take care'; काळजी करू नका 'don't worry'

phrases.en: Is there a clinic near here?

phrases.native: दिवसातून तीन वेळा ही गोळी घ्या.
phrases.roman: divasātūn tīn veḷā hī goḷī ghyā.
phrases.en: Take this tablet three times a day.

phrases.note: Informal: लवकर बरा हो / बरी हो.

grammar.title: Saying what hurts and how you feel
grammar.body:
Three patterns cover most health talk:

**1. Body part + दुखणे** — the body part is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: माझं डोकं दुखतंय (n), माझा पाय दुखतोय (m), माझी पाठ दुखतेय (f), माझे डोळे दुखतायत (pl). For internal pain use -त: पोटात दुखतंय.

**2. मला + illness + आहे / झाला** — मला ताप आहे 'I have a fever', मला सर्दी झाली आहे 'I've got a cold' (झाली agrees with सर्दी, f).

**3. मला + adjective/adverb + वाटणे** — मला बरं वाटतंय 'I feel well', मला बरं वाटत नाही 'I don't feel well', मला थंडी वाजतेय 'I feel cold'.

The forms in -तंय / -तोय / -तेय are colloquial present continuous ('is hurting') — see Unit 10.

examples.en: The child has got a cough.

grammar.title: 'Should': -आवं and -आयला हवं
grammar.body:
**Stem + आवा / आवी / आवं** expresses 'should / ought to'. With a transitive verb it agrees with the **object**; with no object, use neuter **-आवं**: तुम्ही आराम करावा (आराम m), तुम्ही औषध घ्यावं (औषध n), ही गोळी घ्यावी (f), तुम्ही झोपावं 'you should sleep'.

**Stem + आयला हवं / पाहिजे** is the everyday spoken 'should / need to': तुम्ही डॉक्टरकडे जायला हवं 'you should go to the doctor'.

**'Shouldn't':** stem + **ऊ नये**: थंड पाणी पिऊ नये 'one shouldn't drink cold water'. Commands: **करू नका** (polite) / **करू नकोस** (informal) 'don't do'.

examples.en: You should go to the doctor.
You need to drink more water.
You shouldn't eat cold things when you have a fever.

dialogue.title: At the clinic
dialogue.setting: Kiran visits the family doctor in Pune.

lines.speaker: Kiran
lines.en: I've had a fever for two days, doctor.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.en: Do you have a cough as well?

lines.speaker: Kiran
lines.en: Yes, and my throat hurts too.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: घसा लाल झाला आहे. व्हायरल इन्फेक्शन आहे.
lines.roman: ghasā lāl dzhālā āhe. vhāyral infekshan āhe.
lines.en: Your throat is red. It's a viral infection.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: नाही, काळजी करू नका. ही औषधं तीन दिवस घ्या.
lines.roman: nāhī, kāḷjī karū nakā. hī aushadhaṃ tīn divas ghyā.
lines.en: No, don't worry. Take these medicines for three days.

lines.speaker: Doctor
lines.native: आणि भरपूर पाणी प्या, आराम करा.
lines.roman: āṇi bharpūr pāṇī pyā, ārām karā.
lines.en: And drink plenty of water and rest.

culture: Many Marathi families have a trusted family doctor (फॅमिली डॉक्टर) and a stock of home remedies: हळद-दूध (turmeric milk) for a cough, आलं-तुळशीचा चहा (ginger-basil tea) for a cold, and lots of advice about 'hot' and 'cold' foods. Doctors are addressed simply as डॉक्टर or डॉक्टरसाहेब and referred to with respectful plural forms.
